topic: Forecasting weekly fresh produce demand for a small grocery chain with gradient boosting.
work:
Title: Forecasting weekly demand for fresh produce in a small grocery chain

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A regional grocery chain with nine stores throws away about one tenth of its fresh produce each week because orders are placed from a simple moving average. Store managers and the chain's buyers are affected, through lost margin and empty shelves.
Research question. Can gradient boosting forecast weekly demand for fresh produce more accurately than the chain's current moving-average method? Second, does adding local weather data improve those forecasts?
Objectives.
1. Build a baseline moving-average forecast for ten produce items.
2. Train and tune a gradient boosting model on two years of sales.
3. Test whether weather variables improve accuracy.
Expected contribution. The work gives the chain a tested forecasting approach it can adopt, and adds evidence on whether weather data is worth collecting for small retailers.
Pathway. Predictive Modelling

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A comparative model study using historical sales split by time.
Data. Weekly sales for ten produce items across nine stores from January 2024 to June 2026 (about 4,000 rows), provided under a written access agreement signed on 18 September 2026, plus public weather records from the national weather service.
Method. A moving-average baseline, gradient boosting with time-series cross-validation (objectives 1 and 2), and the same model with weather variables added (objective 3).
Evaluation. I will compare mean absolute percentage error against the chain's current moving-average forecast on a held-out final eight weeks.
Feasibility. The main risk is missing sales weeks caused by store system outages. I will fill gaps with the previous year's value and report how many were filled.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Model building and tuning: December 2026 to January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Weather experiment and write-up: March to April 2027
M4 Final submission: 28 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Retail forecasting studies mostly use large supermarkets and daily data (Adler, 2019; Bianchi, 2020). Few test small chains with short sales histories, and weather is rarely compared on equal terms (Costa, 2021). My project responds to this gap.

References

topic: Using simulation to shorten order picking time in a distribution warehouse.

Title: Reducing order picking time in a mid-sized distribution warehouse

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. Pickers at a mid-sized distribution warehouse walk long, uneven routes, and customers wait longer for orders at peak times. Warehouse staff and customers are both affected.
Research question. Which changes to the slotting of fast-moving items would shorten average picking time per order the most?
Objectives.
1. Map the current picking routes from scanner logs.
2. Simulate three alternative slotting layouts.
3. Compare the layouts on time per order.
4. Estimate the saving in picker hours per week.
5. Recommend a staffing rule for peak days.
Expected contribution. A reusable simulation approach and a ranked list of layout changes for the warehouse.
Pathway. Process and Operations Analytics

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A simulation study built on observed picking logs.
Data. I will use the picking logs of a large logistics company, which I have not yet contacted but expect to obtain.
Method. Route mapping (objective 1), discrete-event simulation (objectives 2 and 4) and a comparison of layouts with paired tests (objective 3).
Evaluation. I will judge whether the results look sensible and useful to the warehouse.
Feasibility. The main risk is that the simulation takes longer than planned, so I will build the simplest layout first and add detail only if time allows.

Title: Why subscribers cancel a meal-kit service: a survey-based churn study

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A meal-kit subscription company loses about a third of new subscribers within three months. Its marketing and product teams do not know whether price, variety or delivery problems drive cancellations, so retention offers are guesses.
Research question. Which reasons for cancelling are most common among subscribers who leave within three months?
Objectives.
1. Survey recent former subscribers about their reasons for leaving.
2. Group the reasons into themes and rank them.
3. Compare the themes between price-driven and delivery-driven leavers.
Expected contribution. The company gets an evidence-based list of churn reasons, and the study adds a small data point on early churn in subscription food services.

Design. A cross-sectional online survey with a short follow-up interview.
Data. A survey of 150 former subscribers, recruited by e-mail through the company's mailing list under a written access agreement dated 25 September 2026.
Method. Thematic coding of open answers (objective 2) and a chi-square test of theme frequencies between groups (objective 3).
Evaluation. Success means at least 100 completed surveys and a top-ranked theme that differs from the second theme at the 5 percent significance level.

topic: Segmenting the customers of an online furniture shop and comparing their e-mail response.
work:
Title: Segmenting online furniture shoppers by browsing and purchase behaviour

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. An online furniture shop sends the same promotional e-mail to all of its 40,000 customers, and open rates have fallen from 28 percent to 16 percent over two years. The marketing manager and the customers who receive irrelevant offers are affected, and the shop wastes advertising budget on people who are unlikely to buy.
Research question. Which customer segments based on browsing and purchase behaviour respond differently to promotional e-mails?
Objectives.
1. Clean and combine browsing logs and purchase records for the past two years.
2. Build customer segments with clustering methods and describe each segment.
3. Compare e-mail open and purchase rates across the segments.
4. Suggest a targeting plan for the next three campaigns.
Expected contribution. The shop receives a segment profile it can use to target its campaigns, and the study adds to the limited evidence on e-mail response among small online retailers.
Pathway. Customer and Market Analytics

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A segmentation study on historical records, followed by a comparison of response rates across the segments that are found.
Data. The customer records come from a family friend who runs an online furniture shop. I have not agreed anything in writing yet, but I will ask once the proposal is approved. The shop would remove names and e-mail addresses before sharing.
Method. I will use k-means and hierarchical clustering after standardising the variables (objective 2), choose the number of segments with silhouette scores (objective 2), and compare segment response rates with chi-square tests (objective 3). I will also try a Gaussian mixture model if time allows.
Evaluation. Segments will be judged on a silhouette score of at least 0.4, stability across two random samples of customers, and a difference in open rate of at least five percentage points between the best and the worst segment.
Feasibility. The main risk is that the browsing logs are incomplete before March 2025, because the shop changed its web platform then. If so, I will limit the data to the period after the change, and I will report what this does to the sample size and to the confidence in each segment.

Part 3: Preliminary timeline
M1 Proposal submission: 9 October 2026
M2 Data secured: 27 November 2026
Data cleaning and exploratory analysis: December 2026
Clustering experiments: January 2027
M3 Interim report: 12 February 2027
Response comparison and targeting plan: March to April 2027
Report writing and checking: April to May 2027
M4 Final submission: 14 May 2027

Part 4: References and critical literature summary
Customer segmentation is well developed for large retailers (Adler, 2019; Bianchi, 2020), mostly using purchase history alone. Browsing data is rarely combined with purchase data for small shops, and the link from segments to e-mail response is seldom tested (Costa, 2021). My project responds to this gap in the existing work.

topic: A process mining study of waiting-time bottlenecks in one outpatient clinic.

Title: A Comprehensive Process Mining Study of Patient Waiting Time Bottlenecks and Scheduling Inefficiencies in Outpatient Clinics Across a Regional Network

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. Patients at a regional outpatient clinic wait on average 48 minutes beyond their appointment time, according to the clinic's own survey. Patients, nurses and doctors are all affected.
Research question. Which steps in the outpatient visit create the longest waiting times?
Objectives.
1. Extract event logs from the appointment system.
2. Map the visit process with process mining.
3. Identify the three steps that add the most delay.
Expected contribution. The clinic gets a data-based list of its main delay points, and the study adds a small case to the process mining literature on outpatient care.
Pathway. Process and Operations Analytics

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A process mining case study of one clinic.
Data. Anonymised appointment event logs from one clinic for 2025 (about 30,000 visits), released under a written data sharing agreement dated 6 October 2026.
Method. Event log cleaning (objective 1), process discovery (objective 2) and bottleneck analysis by step (objective 3).
Evaluation. The analysis succeeds if the three identified steps together account for at least 60 percent of total waiting time in the logs, checked against a manual sample of 100 visits.
Feasibility. There are three risks: the logs may be incomplete, the clinic may withdraw its consent, and process mining software may be hard to learn.

Title: Forecasting energy use in office buildings

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. Facility managers of large office buildings cannot plan electricity purchases because daily use swings with weather and occupancy. Facility managers and building owners are affected through unpredictable costs.
Research question. How accurately can daily electricity use in office buildings be predicted from occupancy and weather data?
Objectives.
1. Prepare a daily dataset of electricity use, occupancy and weather.
2. Train regression and tree-based models on the first year of data.
3. Test the accuracy of each model on a held-out second year.

Design. A comparative model study on public building data.

Method. I will fit a regularised linear regression (objective 2) and a random forest (objective 2). I will also train a deep neural network and a transformer model, because they are popular.

work:
Title: Price sensitivity of e-bike rental demand in a mid-sized city

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. A city e-bike rental operator changes its hourly price a few times a year but does not know how riders respond at different times of day. The operator and its riders are affected by prices that may be too high at peaks or too low off-peak.
Research question. How does the hourly rental price affect e-bike demand at different times of day?
Objectives.
1. Estimate how rental demand changes with price.
Expected contribution. A tested estimate of price sensitivity that the operator can use in its next price review, and a worked example for other small mobility firms.
Pathway. Customer and Market Analytics and Predictive Modelling

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A natural experiment based on past price changes, plus a short rider survey.
Data. The public trip dataset published on the city's open data portal for 2024 and 2025 (about 1.2 million trips) plus a short intercept survey of 80 riders at stations.
Method. A log-log regression of trips on price with time-of-day effects (objective 1), and a descriptive summary of the survey answers.
Evaluation. The model must explain at least 60 percent of the variation in hourly trips on a held-out month, and price effects must be significant at the 5 percent level.
Feasibility. The main risk is that price changes coincide with seasons, so I will include month effects and test the result on one unaffected district.

work:
Title: Predicting late invoice payments for small design agencies

Part 1: Description of the intended work
Problem. Small design agencies often wait more than 30 days for invoices to be paid, and the delay strains their cash flow. Agency owners are affected, because they cannot tell which clients will pay late.
Research question. Can invoice and client details predict which invoices will be paid more than 30 days late?
Objectives.
1. Prepare a modelling dataset from a public invoice collection.
2. Fit a logistic regression model to flag late payments.
3. Compare it with a gradient boosting model on held-out invoices.
Expected contribution. Small agencies get a simple way to spot risky invoices early, and the study adds evidence on which invoice details signal late payment.
Pathway. Predictive Modelling

Part 2: Methodological approach
Design. A comparative model study on anonymised invoice records.
Data. A public anonymised dataset of 90,000 small-business invoices released by an open payments project, free to download.
Method. Logistic regression (objective 2) and gradient boosting (objective 3), with a simple rule-based baseline for comparison.
Evaluation. Models are compared on the area under the ROC curve on a held-out final quarter, and the aim is to beat a rule that flags every invoice over 30 days old by at least 0.05.
Feasibility. The main risk is class imbalance, because only about one invoice in eight is paid late. I will test oversampling and report results with and without it.
